Introduction An entrepreneur needs capital and has to provide effort to advance the success of their business. Capital can be raised primarily as debt or equity, however, hybrid instruments might also be available. In this paper, we focus on a near-equity financial instrument known as musharaka in Islamic finance.1 A musharaka contract results in profit and loss sharing not unlike a partnership with an equity investor. Musharaka is, however, more similar to project financing in which the investor provides capital to be invested in some particular tangible assets or a joint venture (Jobst, 2017), and the profits and losses from this particular project are shared. In contrast, providing equity capital results in co-ownership of the entire business, and the equity holders share all profits or losses and any increase or decrease in total value of the firm. Therefore, musharaka and equity financing differ with respect to risk sharing and result in different incentives for the entrepreneur. We compare the alternative financial contracts in an agency-theoretic model with risk sharing and managerial incentives for the entrepreneur as the main determinants of the entrepreneur's utility. We start with debt financing and then consider musharaka and equity financing from the perspective of an entrepreneur in a principal-agent relationship. The direct comparison of musharaka and equity financing reveals no definite ranking. The partial profit and loss sharing via musharaka financing, that is, the sharing of profits and losses arising not from the whole business, but from a particular project or certain assets only, results in suboptimal risk sharing. On the other hand, musharaka comes with better incentives for the entrepreneur and results in a higher increase in expected firm value net of (private) costs under certain conditions. DOI: 10.4236/me.2026.171001 PDF HTML XML 60 Downloads 565 Views Citations Abstract Islamic finance products and services directly reflect the real economy. The main reason they are not based on the appreciation of money, however, could be sales (murabahah, salam, istisna), leasing (Ijarah), investment (wakala), partnership methods (musharakah, mudarabah), or other asset-backed instruments (sukuk). Even though sales via leasing-based financing are widely used, partnership methods (musharakah, mudarabah), which are necessary for the real economy and growth, account for only a small share of total financing. This study aims to analyze musharakah (capital partnership) financing with all aspects, regulations, standards, country cases, and why this method is not used as expected. The answers show that there are no specific differences between countries in rules and practices; however, the reasons behind comparatively lower musharakah financing are the same. To channel resources directly into production and investment, possible risks need to be reduced, control mechanisms strengthened, and the human resources empowered. Keywords Musharakah Financing & Obstacles, Islamic Finance Musharakah Standards, Islamic Finance Partnership Methods Share and Cite: Demirtaş, T. (2026) Evaluation of Musharakah Financing, Standards, Country Cases, Major Obstacles and Solutions —A Study of Islamic Finance Partnership Methods. Modern Economy, 17, 1-13. doi: 10.4236/me.2026.171001. 1. Introduction Islamic finance products and services are different from conventional ones. The primary reason is that all financing products are interest-free and backed by assets, sales, trading, investments, projects, and the real economy rather than by pure money transactions. As a result, products and services directly affect the real economy. These transactions could be on sales methods (murabahah, salam, istisna), leasing methods (Ijarah), investment methods (wakala), partnership methods (musharakah, mudarabah), or other asset-backed methods (sukuk). However, while some products (murabahah, ijara, tawarruq) are widely used, some others (musharakah, mudharabah) are not preferred as expected (Demirtaş, 2024a). The partnership methods (musharakah, mudharabah), which support projects and investments, are essential to the real economy and growth but account for only a small share of total financing. This study aims to analyze one partnership method, musharakah structure, regulations, country cases with data, and the reasons why this financing method is rarely used. In this study, the first section explains what musharakah is and the main differences between other partnership methods, mudarabahah, from musharakah. Musharakah is coming from the word “sharaka”, which means partnership, share, participate, or be a partner. Musharakah (capital partnership) differs from other partnership methods, mudarabah (labor-capital partnership), in that each partner contributes cash or in-kind capital. The profits resulting from the partnership are shared according to the initially agreed profit-sharing ratios, while losses are shared in proportion to the parties’ capital contributions. The second section discusses international regulations and standards on musharakah and how countries implement them in practice. AAOIFI and IFSB are the major regulators in the international arena, and they are generally principle-based rather than rule-based. The third section analyses the financing structure of 11 major countries, the distribution of the products, and the musharakah position. The data show that Islamic countries widely use sale-based murabaha; however, the share of partnership products, musharakah (capital partnership), and mudarabah (capital-labor share), is less preferred. The asset-based and buy-and-sell structure of murabahah makes these products less risky and more practical in the Islamic financial system. Today, approximately 50 percent of total fund allocations and transfers are done in this way. On the other hand, the average is only 13 percent for musharakah. Branch report: basic structure and principles of Islamic profit-sharing contracts

Islamic profit-sharing contracts are typically structured around two major forms: **mudarabah** and **musharakah**. In mudarabah, one party provides capital (the *rabb-ul-maal*) and the other provides management or entrepreneurial effort (the *mudarib*), with profits shared according to a pre-agreed ratio. In musharakah, multiple parties contribute capital or other resources and share profits and losses in proportion to their contributions [N2-R1][N2-R5][N3-F2]. These contracts are not limited to one form; the evidence also notes that profit-sharing in both mudarabah and musharakah is guided by mutual consent and transparent agreement on proportions at contract formation [N1-R5].

The core Islamic principles that make profit-sharing permissible are rooted in **equity, risk-sharing, and asset-backed real-economy engagement**. The Pepperdine article states that Islamic profit-sharing contracts adhere most closely to the three principles underlying Islamic finance: equity, wealth distribution, and the rejection of interest-based transactions [N1-R1]. It also emphasizes that Islamic finance avoids interest and speculation, instead favoring risk-sharing and asset-backed structures [N1-F1]. The same source explains that musharaka financing is more like a partnership with an equity investor, while debt financing is inferior to musharaka and equity in some contexts because it foregoes the benefits of risk sharing [N1-F1]. This shows that profit-sharing is not just a commercial mechanism but a doctrinal choice that aligns with Islamic finance’s broader rejection of riba and emphasis on shared risk and real economic activity.

Risk and return are treated differently from conventional finance because Islamic profit-sharing contracts are designed to avoid **fixed returns on capital** and instead tie returns to performance and shared risk. In mudarabah, the rabb-ul-maal provides capital, while the mudarib provides management; profits are shared according to a pre-agreed ratio, but losses are not typically distributed in the same way as fixed income [N2-R5][N3-R2]. The evidence also notes that mudarabah is used mostly by banks, where the bank can act both as an investor and as an entrepreneur, indicating a hybrid model in which the financier also bears some operational responsibility [N2-R2]. In musharaka, profits are shared according to initially agreed ratios, and losses are shared in proportion to capital contributions [N3-F2]. This contrasts with conventional finance, where debt often guarantees a fixed return for capital, while equity ties returns to overall firm performance. The Pepperdine paper explicitly compares musharaka with equity and debt, showing that Islamic profit-sharing is meant to balance incentives and risk sharing rather than simply replicating conventional equity-like ownership [N1-F1].

Overall, the structure of Islamic profit-sharing contracts is built on **mutual consent, transparent profit-sharing ratios, and shared risk**, while the principles that make them permissible are rooted in equity, asset-backedness, and the rejection of interest and speculation [N1-R1][N1-R5][N1-F1].

Branch report: roles of parties in profit-sharing contracts

In Islamic profit-sharing contracts, the parties are usually divided into two broad roles: **capital contributor(s)** and **manager/entrepreneur**. In mudarabah, the capital provider is called the *rabb-ul-maal*, and the manager is the *mudarib*; in musharakah, multiple parties contribute capital or other resources, and the roles are more collaborative [N2-R1][N2-R5][N3-F2]. The evidence also notes that mudarabah is a partnership where one party provides capital and the other manages the investment or business, while musharakah is a joint venture [N2-R1][N2-R3]. This distinction is important because it defines who is responsible for what and how authority is distributed.

The legal roles of each party are relatively clear. In mudarabah, the *rabb-ul-maal* is responsible for providing the capital, while the *mudarib* is responsible for managing the business or investment [N2-R1][N2-R5]. The Blossom Finance source explicitly states that both parties must agree on the profit-sharing ratio at contract formation [N2-R3]. In musharakah, the parties contribute capital or in-kind resources, and profits are shared according to agreed ratios while losses are shared in proportion to capital contributions [N3-F2]. This implies that each party’s role is tied to their contribution and that their responsibilities are limited to the scope of their contribution. The evidence also notes that mudarabah is used mostly by banks, where the bank can act both as an investor and as an entrepreneur, suggesting that in practice the roles may overlap, but the legal principle remains that capital and management are distinct [N2-R2].

Responsibilities and limitations are also clearly defined. The *rabb-ul-maal* in mudarabah is generally not liable for losses unless the mudarib misuses the capital or the contract has specific provisions to the contrary [N2-R3][N3-F2]. The mudarib, by contrast, is responsible for managing the business, but is not typically liable for the capital itself [N2-R1][N3-F2]. In musharakah, the parties share losses in proportion to their capital contributions, so each party’s liability is proportional to their stake [N3-F2]. The evidence also emphasizes that all mudarabahs are independent of one another, and none is liable for the liabilities of any other mudarabah [N4-R5]. This separation of liability is a key limitation on the manager or entrepreneur in mudarabah.

Ownership and capital contribution affect decision power in a direct way. In musharakah, where multiple parties contribute capital, the evidence suggests that decision power is shared in proportion to capital contribution [N3-F2]. In mudarabah, the manager (*mudarib*) typically has operational authority, but the capital provider has a separate role as financier rather than decision-maker [N2-R1][N2-R5]. The Pepperdine source also indicates that musharaka is more like a partnership with an equity investor, implying that the capital owner may have some voice in major decisions [N1-F1]. However, the evidence does not provide a detailed breakdown of decision-making authority across jurisdictions, so this conclusion remains context-dependent [N1-F1].

In summary, the parties in Islamic profit-sharing contracts are usually capital contributors and managers, with roles, responsibilities, and liabilities clearly separated. Mudarabah separates capital from management, while musharakah shares both capital and decision-making in proportion to contributions [N2-R1][N2-R5][N3-F2]. Ownership and capital contribution thus shape decision power, but the evidence here is stronger on separation of roles than on a universal governance model [N2-R3][N3-F2].

Islamic profit-sharing contracts allocate profits and losses according to pre-agreed ratios, with the key rule being that **profits are distributed based on agreed share of actual profit rather than a fixed cash return**. The evidence states that it is necessary in mudarabah that both parties agree on the profit-sharing ratio at contract formation, and that the distribution of profit must be on the basis of the percentage of profit [N2-R3][N3-R2]. The Pepperdine article similarly notes that musharaka contracts result in profit and loss sharing, and that profit-sharing in both mudarabah and musharakah is guided by mutual consent and transparent agreement on proportions [N1-R5]. In practice, a common ratio is a pre-agreed percentage, such as 60:40, where the capital provider gets 60% and the manager gets 40% [N3-R4].

Profits are allocated to each party according to the **initially agreed profit-sharing ratios**. In musharakah, profits are shared according to the initially agreed profit-sharing ratios, while losses are shared in proportion to the parties’ capital contributions [N3-F2]. In mudarabah, the evidence says that profits are shared according to the initially agreed profit-sharing ratio, and that losses are not typically distributed in the same way as fixed income [N2-R5]. The Blossom Finance source also says that profit distribution must be on the basis of the percentage of profit, which supports the idea that distribution is tied to actual performance rather than a predetermined cash entitlement [N2-R3]. The Facebook excerpt from Meezan Bank reinforces this by stating that mudarabah is a profit-sharing partnership where the customer and the bank share profit according to a pre-agreed ratio [N2-R4].

Losses are handled differently from profits. In musharakah, losses are shared in proportion to the parties’ capital contributions, meaning that each party bears loss proportional to their stake [N3-F2]. In mudarabah, the evidence indicates that losses are attributed to the capital owner, while the laborer’s losses are attributed to the capital owner; the exact wording is incomplete, but the general principle is that the capital provider bears the burden of loss [N2-R5]. The Blossom Finance source also notes that in mudarabah, losses are not distributed in the same way as fixed income, which implies that losses are borne by the capital side rather than being shared or distributed as a separate obligation [N2-R3]. Common formulas or ratios used in practice are typically **pre-agreed profit-sharing ratios**. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that the parties must agree on the ratio at contract formation, with examples such as 60:40 or 50:50 [N2-R3][N3-R4]. The Pepperdine paper notes that musharaka is a near-equity financial instrument, which supports the use of partnership-style ratios rather than a fixed-cash return model [N1-F1]. The study on musharakah financing also says that profits are shared according to initially agreed profit-sharing ratios, while losses are shared in proportion to capital contributions, showing that the practical formula is a combination of agreed ratio and proportional loss allocation [N3-F2].

In short, profit distribution in Islamic profit-sharing contracts is based on **pre-agreed profit-sharing ratios**, with losses typically handled by the capital provider or in proportion to capital contributions. The common practice is to use a transparent, agreed percentage rather than a fixed return, and the evidence strongly supports this structure across mudarabah and musharakah [N2-R3][N2-R5][N3-F2].

The evidence indicates that **decision control is usually shared or limited** rather than fully centralized. This suggests that decision-making is not tied to a single party’s ownership stake in the conventional sense, but rather to the roles and contributions of the parties.

The evidence does not provide a single universal governance rule, but it does indicate that **control is shared or limited in proportion to capital contribution**. In musharakah, because each party contributes capital, the study says that profits and losses are shared according to the parties’ capital contributions, implying that decision-making is likely shared in line with ownership structure [N3-F2]. In mudarabah, the manager has operational authority, but the capital provider has a separate role as financier rather than decision-maker [N2-R1][N2-R5]. The Pepperdine article also notes that musharaka is more like a partnership with an equity investor, which implies that the capital owner may have some voice in major decisions [N1-F1]. Overall, decision control and governance in Islamic profit-sharing contracts are shaped by the contract type, the balance of capital and management, and the broader Sharia and regulatory framework. In mudarabah, the manager has operational authority, while the capital provider has a separate role; in musharakah, control is likely shared in proportion to capital contribution; and in both cases, Sharia-compliant governance and regulatory frameworks may require additional mechanisms to ensure enforceability and accountability [N2-R1][N2-R5][N3-F2][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R4].

# How profit-sharing participation contracts operate in Islamic finance

Islamic profit-sharing participation contracts are the core mechanism through which Islamic finance avoids interest-based returns and instead ties returns to shared risk and performance. These contracts are typically structured around two major forms: **mudarabah** and **musharakah**. Mudarabah is a partnership where one party provides capital and the other provides management, while musharakah is a joint venture in which multiple parties contribute capital or other resources and share profits and losses accordingly [N2-R1][N2-R5][N3-F2]. The evidence also notes that profit-sharing in both mudarabah and musharakah is guided by mutual consent and transparent agreement on proportions at contract formation [N1-R5]. This shows that Islamic profit-sharing is not merely a commercial arrangement but a principled contract model.

## 1) Basic structure and principles

### What types of contracts are used?
Islamic profit-sharing contracts primarily use **mudarabah** and **musharakah**. Mudarabah separates capital and management, with the capital provider (*rabb-ul-maal*) and the manager (*mudarib*), while musharakah is a collaborative partnership where multiple parties contribute capital or other resources [N2-R1][N2-R5][N3-F2]. The evidence also notes that mudarabah is used mostly by banks, where the bank can act both as an investor and as an entrepreneur, indicating a hybrid model in which the financier also bears some operational responsibility [N2-R2].

### Core Islamic principles
The core Islamic principles that make profit-sharing permissible are **equity, risk-sharing, and asset-backed real-economy engagement**. The Pepperdine article states that Islamic profit-sharing contracts adhere most closely to the three principles underlying Islamic finance: equity, wealth distribution, and the rejection of interest-based transactions [N1-R1]. It also emphasizes that Islamic finance avoids interest and speculation, instead favoring risk-sharing and asset-backed structures [N1-F1]. The same source compares musharaka with equity and debt, showing that Islamic profit-sharing is meant to balance incentives and risk sharing rather than simply replicating conventional equity-like ownership [N1-F1].

### How risk and return differ from conventional finance
Risk and return are treated differently because Islamic profit-sharing contracts are designed to avoid **fixed returns on capital** and instead tie returns to performance and shared risk. In mudarabah, the *rabb-ul-maal* provides capital, while the *mudarib* provides management; profits are shared according to a pre-agreed ratio, but losses are not typically distributed in the same way as fixed income [N2-R5][N3-R2]. In musharakah, profits are shared according to initially agreed profit-sharing ratios, and losses are shared in proportion to the parties’ capital contributions [N3-F2]. This contrasts with conventional finance, where debt often guarantees a fixed return for capital, while equity ties returns to overall firm performance. The evidence also shows that musharaka is more like a partnership with an equity investor, implying that Islamic profit-sharing contracts operate closer to partnership-style structures than to conventional debt-equity hybrids [N1-F1].

## 2) Roles of the parties involved

### Which parties are involved and their legal roles
In Islamic profit-sharing contracts, the parties are usually divided into two broad roles: **capital contributor(s)** and **manager/entrepreneur**. In mudarabah, the capital provider is the *rabb-ul-maal*, and the manager is the *mudarib*; in musharakah, multiple parties contribute capital or other resources, and the roles are more collaborative [N2-R1][N2-R5][N3-F2]. The evidence also notes that mudarabah is a partnership where one party provides capital and the other manages the investment or business, while musharakah is a joint venture [N2-R1][N2-R3]. This distinction is important because it defines who is responsible for what and how authority is distributed.

### Responsibilities and limitations
The legal roles are relatively clear. In mudarabah, the *rabb-ul-maal* is responsible for providing the capital, while the *mudarib* is responsible for managing the business or investment [N2-R1][N2-R5]. The Blossom Finance source explicitly states that both parties must agree on the profit-sharing ratio at contract formation [N2-R3]. In musharakah, the parties contribute capital or in-kind resources, and profits are shared according to agreed ratios while losses are shared in proportion to capital contributions [N3-F2]. This implies that each party’s responsibilities are tied to their contribution.

The evidence also notes that all mudarabahs are independent of one another, and none is liable for the liabilities of, or is entitled to benefit from, the assets of any other mudarabah [N4-R5]. This separation of liability is a key limitation on the manager or entrepreneur in mudarabah. In musharakah, the evidence suggests that losses are shared in proportion to capital contributions, so each party’s liability is proportional to their stake [N3-F2]. The mudarabah evidence also indicates that the capital provider is not liable for losses unless the manager misuses the capital, which further limits liability [N2-R3].

### How ownership and capital contribution affect decision power
Ownership and capital contribution affect decision power in a direct way. In musharakah, where multiple parties contribute capital, the evidence suggests that decision power is shared in proportion to capital contribution [N3-F2]. In mudarabah, the manager typically has operational authority, but the capital provider has a separate role as financier rather than decision-maker [N2-R1][N2-R5]. The Pepperdine source also indicates that musharaka is more like a partnership with an equity investor, implying that the capital owner may have some voice in major decisions [N1-F1]. However, the evidence does not provide a detailed breakdown of decision-making authority across jurisdictions, so this conclusion remains context-dependent [N1-F1].

## 3) Profit distribution rules

Islamic profit-sharing contracts allocate profits and losses according to pre-agreed ratios. The key rule is that **profits are distributed based on agreed share of actual profit rather than a fixed cash return**. The evidence states that it is necessary in mudarabah that both parties agree on the profit-sharing ratio at contract formation, and that the distribution of profit must be on the basis of the percentage of profit [N2-R3][N3-R2]. The Pepperdine article similarly notes that profit-sharing in both mudarabah and musharakah is guided by mutual consent and transparent agreement on proportions [N1-R5]. In practice, a common ratio is a pre-agreed percentage, such as 60:40, where the capital provider gets 60% and the manager gets 40% [N3-R4].

Profits are allocated to each party according to the **initially agreed profit-sharing ratios**. In musharakah, profits are shared according to the initially agreed profit-sharing ratios, while losses are shared in proportion to the parties’ capital contributions [N3-F2]. In mudarabah, the evidence says that profits are shared according to the initially agreed profit-sharing ratio, and that losses are not typically distributed in the same way as fixed income [N2-R5]. The Blossom Finance source also says that profit distribution must be on the basis of the percentage of profit, which supports the idea that distribution is tied to actual performance rather than a predetermined cash entitlement [N2-R3]. The Meezan Bank excerpt reinforces this by stating that mudarabah is a profit-sharing partnership where the customer and the bank share profit according to a pre-agreed ratio [N2-R4].

Losses are handled differently from profits. In musharakah, losses are shared in proportion to the parties’ capital contributions, meaning that each party bears loss proportional to their stake [N3-F2]. In mudarabah, the evidence indicates that losses are attributed to the capital owner, while the laborer’s losses are attributed to the capital owner; the exact wording is incomplete, but the general principle is that the capital provider bears the burden of loss [N2-R5]. The Blossom Finance source also notes that in mudarabah, losses are not distributed in the same way as fixed income, which implies that losses are borne by the capital side rather than being shared or distributed as a separate obligation [N2-R3].

Common formulas or ratios used in practice are typically **pre-agreed profit-sharing ratios**. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that the parties must agree on the ratio at contract formation, with examples such as 60:40 or 50:50 [N2-R3][N3-R4]. The Pepperdine paper notes that musharaka is a near-equity financial instrument, which supports the use of partnership-style ratios rather than a fixed-cash return model [N1-F1]. The study on musharakah financing also says that profits are shared according to initially agreed profit-sharing ratios, while losses are shared in proportion to capital contributions, showing that the practical formula is a combination of agreed ratio and proportional loss allocation [N3-F2].

## 4) Control over business decisions

Who gets to make major business decisions depends on the contract type and the balance of capital and management. The evidence indicates that **decision control is usually shared or limited** rather than fully centralized. In mudarabah, the capital provider provides capital, while the manager manages the business; the source notes that mudarabah is a partnership where one party provides capital and the other manages the investment or business [N2-R1][N2-R5]. In musharakah, multiple parties contribute capital, and the evidence states that profits are shared according to initially agreed profit-sharing ratios, while losses are shared in proportion to capital contributions [N3-F2]. This suggests that decision-making is not tied to a single party’s ownership stake in the conventional sense, but rather to the roles and contributions of the parties.

The evidence does not provide a single universal governance rule, but it does indicate that **control is shared or limited in proportion to capital contribution**. In musharakah, because each party contributes capital, the study says that profits and losses are shared according to the parties’ capital contributions, implying that decision-making is likely shared in line with ownership structure [N3-F2]. In mudarabah, the manager has operational authority, but the capital provider has a separate role as financier rather than decision-maker [N2-R1][N2-R5]. The Pepperdine article also notes that musharaka is more like a partnership with an equity investor, which implies that the capital owner may have some voice in major decisions [N1-F1]. However, the evidence is thinner on the exact mechanisms of voting, consensus, or formal governance structures.

The context provided by the Islamic finance governance material is important. It notes that regulators mandate Sharia governance frameworks, including boards, audits, and compliance structures, and that Islamic finance principles emphasize risk-sharing and asset-based financing [N4-R1][N4-R2]. The evidence also mentions that the sharia Federal Court is the highest authority for sharia matters in Pakistan, and that Islamic financial institutions are subject to Sharia governance frameworks [N4-R4]. This background context supports the idea that decision control is not left entirely to informal agreement; instead, it is shaped by formal Sharia-compliant governance mechanisms and regulatory expectations [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R4].

Consensus or additional mechanisms may be required depending on the jurisdiction and the contract. The evidence does not provide a detailed checklist of consensus rules, but it does indicate that **Islamic finance contracts are typically principle-based** and that regulators and Sharia authorities play a role in ensuring compliance [N4-R2][N4-R4]. The musharakah study also emphasizes that possible risks need to be reduced, control mechanisms strengthened, and human resources empowered, suggesting that governance is an active concern rather than an afterthought [N3-F2]. In this sense, major business decisions may require consultation, approval, or formal governance procedures when the contract is structured under Sharia-compliant frameworks [N4-R2][N4-R4].

## 5) Contractual mechanics, liability, and enforceability

Islamic profit-sharing contracts require several terms to be clearly defined at contract formation. The most important are **profit-sharing ratio, capital contribution, management role, risk allocation, and loss-sharing mechanism**. The Blossom Finance source explicitly states that both parties must agree on the profit-sharing ratio at contract formation [N2-R3]. The Pepperdine article similarly notes that profit-sharing in both mudarabah and musharakah is guided by mutual consent and transparent agreement on proportions [N1-R5]. In musharakah, the evidence says profits are shared according to initially agreed profit-sharing ratios, while losses are shared in proportion to capital contributions [N3-F2]. This implies that the contract must also specify how losses are allocated and what each party contributes in terms of capital or resources [N3-F2]. The mudarabah evidence also notes that one party provides capital and the other provides management, reinforcing the need to define roles at the outset [N2-R1][N2-R5].

Liability between parties is separated in a way that protects the capital provider from the operational risks of the manager. In mudarabah, the evidence states that all mudarabahs are independent of one another, and none is liable for the liabilities of, or is entitled to benefit from, the assets of any other mudarabah [N4-R5]. This is a strong separation of liability, meaning that the capital provider’s liability is limited to their own contribution and not to the liabilities of other mudarabahs. In musharakah, the evidence indicates that losses are shared in proportion to capital contributions, so each party’s liability is tied to their stake rather than being unlimited or unbounded [N3-F2]. The mudarabah source also says that the capital provider is not liable for losses unless the manager misuses the capital, which further limits liability [N2-R3].

Sharia and legal mechanisms support enforceability through **Sharia governance frameworks, regulatory requirements, and principle-based contract design**. The Islamic finance governance material states that regulators mandate Sharia governance frameworks, including boards, audits, and compliance structures, and that Islamic finance principles emphasize risk-sharing and asset-based financing [N4-R1][N4-R2]. It also notes that the sharia Federal Court is the highest authority for sharia matters in Pakistan, indicating that Sharia courts or authorities can validate and enforce Islamic finance contracts [N4-R4]. The Chambers Practice Guides evidence similarly notes that regulators recognize Islamic contracts such as murabaha, implying that there is a recognized legal infrastructure for Islamic finance [N6-R3]. The evidence on Islamic finance contracting concepts in Malaysia also emphasizes that mudarabah separates responsibility for capital investment and management, supporting the idea that enforceable contracts can be structured around clear separation of duties [N6-R2].

The evidence also supports enforceability through **explicit, principle-based contract drafting**. The Pepperdine article stresses that profit-sharing contracts must be transparent and that the structure of the contract matters for managerial incentives [N1-F1]. The musharakah study says that possible risks need to be reduced, control mechanisms strengthened, and human resources empowered, which suggests that enforceable contracts must include detailed governance and risk-management provisions [N3-F2]. The evidence on Sharia fintech and madhhab differences indicates that Islamic finance operates under distinct legal and interpretive frameworks, but the core mechanism is that contracts are validated by Sharia principles and regulated by Sharia-compliant governance [N5-R2][N5-R3].

## 6) Doctrinal and practical differences across Islamic schools and jurisdictions

The evidence on doctrinal and practical differences indicates that **Islamic finance operates under distinct legal and interpretive frameworks**, but the core profit-sharing model remains broadly recognizable across schools. The evidence notes that there are significant differences between the four Sunni schools in interpreting whether Sharia fintech is truly free from usury, with the Hanafi school being one of the major schools of interpretation [N5-R2]. It also maps how Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi’i, and Hanbali interpretations shape financial regulations across Southeast Asia, Gulf States, South Asia, and North Africa [N5-R3]. The classical Islamic jurisprudence evidence adds that classical Islamic jurists agreed with each other about the prohibition of riba, but they disagreed on methodological points [N5-R5].

This means that while the basic structure of profit-sharing contracts—such as mudarabah and musharakah—remains consistent with the prohibition of riba and the principle of shared risk, the **details of implementation, governance, and enforcement can vary across schools and jurisdictions**. The evidence does not provide a comprehensive comparison of every school’s ruling, so it is safest to say that doctrinal differences exist, but the overall profit-sharing model is grounded in the same Islamic finance principles [N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R5].

## 7) Bottom line

Islamic profit-sharing participation contracts operate through two main contract forms: **mudarabah** and **musharakah**. Mudarabah separates capital and management, while musharakah is a collaborative partnership in which profits and losses are shared in proportion to contributions [N2-R1][N2-R5][N3-F2]. The core principles are **equity, risk-sharing, and asset-backed real-economy engagement**, which make profit-sharing permissible under Islamic law [N1-R1][N1-F1].

The parties involved are usually the **capital contributor(s)** and the **manager/entrepreneur**, with clearly defined roles and responsibilities. In mudarabah, the capital provider is generally not liable for losses unless the manager misuses the capital, while the manager has operational authority [N2-R1][N2-R3]. In musharakah, losses are shared in proportion to capital contributions, so each party’s liability is tied to their stake [N3-F2]. Ownership and capital contribution affect decision power, with musharakah likely sharing control in proportion to contributions and mudarabah giving operational authority to the manager while keeping the capital provider separate [N2-R1][N2-R5][N3-F2].

Profits are distributed according to pre-agreed ratios, while losses are handled separately, usually borne by the capital side or in proportion to contributions [N2-R3][N3-R2][N3-F2]. Common practice uses transparent, agreed percentages such as 60:40 or 50:50 [N2-R3][N3-R4]. Major business decisions are usually shared or limited, with governance shaped by Sharia-compliant frameworks, regulatory requirements, and principle-based contract design [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R4].

Overall, Islamic profit-sharing contracts are designed to avoid interest, tie returns to shared risk, and maintain a clear separation of roles and liabilities. They are supported by Sharia governance, regulatory frameworks, and principle-based contract drafting, but their exact implementation can vary across schools and jurisdictions [N1-R1][N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R4].
